clue.text: Oversee dismantling of decoration

indicators.note: dismantling takes a thing apart, so the letters come to pieces and are rebuilt in another order

parts.note: taken as written; all ten letters are used

explanation.surface: Someone is put in charge of taking down the Christmas decorations.
explanation.walkthrough: DECORATION rearranged gives COORDINATE, using every letter exactly once.
explanation.definitionFit: To coordinate a project is to organise and direct its parts, which is supervising work much as a manager does.

clue.text: Wag sending up vampiric character

indicators.note: in a down clue, sending something up makes it read from bottom to top, so the letters run backwards

parts.note: Drac is a short form of Dracula, the vampire count

explanation.surface: A joker mocks a vampire figure, as if lampooning Dracula.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wag' looks like a verb but it is the noun for a joker; 'sending up' also suggests mockery, though here it reverses the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A card, in old-fashioned British slang, is an amusing, eccentric person, just as a wag is a habitual joker.

clue.text: What might ironically be evens?

parts.note: surface reading: a riddle about even numbers being something contrary
setter's reading: evens is a betting price, one-to-one, and a betting price has the word that means the opposite of even as its name

explanation.walkthrough: In betting, evens is a price where the stake is doubled if you win; the name for any such price is the opposite of even numbers, hence the irony.
explanation.definitionFit: Betting prices, such as two-to-one or evens, are collectively called the bookmaker's odds.

clue.text: Horribly westernised drink that's sweet

indicators.note: something done horribly is botched and mangled, so the letters end up badly jumbled

parts.note: taken as written; eleven letters

explanation.surface: A traveller grumbles that a sickly sweet drink has been badly adapted for Western tastes.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition runs to the end of the clue: 'drink that's sweet' describes the answer as a whole.
explanation.definitionFit: Sauternes or Tokaji are sweet wines served with pudding, so the answer is a sugary alcoholic beverage.

clue.text: Coming with formal wear and very informal wear

parts.note: nigh means near, approaching, as in 'the end is nigh'
a tie is worn with formal dress

explanation.surface: A dress code invitation contrasting black tie with something extremely casual.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Coming with' reads like part of the dress code, but 'Coming' alone gives the first piece and 'with' just glues it to the second.
explanation.definitionFit: A nightdress is worn in bed, about as relaxed as clothing gets, so it is humorously described as extremely casual attire.

clue.text: Worries, scratching head and hair

indicators.note: scratching out the head of a word scrubs away its opening letter

parts.note: stresses are worries or anxieties

explanation.surface: An anxious person scratches their head and tugs at their hair.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Scratching head' paints a worried gesture, but it means dropping the S that starts STRESSES.
explanation.definitionFit: Tresses are long locks of a person's hair, a poetic word for it.

clue.text: Unpleasant air bottled by cosmographer

indicators.note: something bottled is kept inside a container, so the answer sits within the following word

parts.note: letters three to six of this word

explanation.surface: A scientist who maps the cosmos is collecting samples of foul air in bottles.
explanation.walkthrough: A cosmographer studies and maps the universe; the four letters run through the word cosMOGrapher starting at its S.
explanation.definitionFit: Smog is polluted fog laden with smoke and fumes, which makes the atmosphere dirty and disagreeable to breathe.

clue.text: Rich supply Mike with alternative 50 words of praise

parts.note: Mike is M in the NATO phonetic alphabet
an alternative is the other option
L is the Roman numeral for fifty
an ode is a poem praising its subject

explanation.surface: A man called Mike is generous with praise, offering fifty alternative compliments.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mike' looks like a person but it is the radio alphabet's word for one letter; 50 is a Roman numeral.
explanation.definitionFit: A mother lode is the principal vein of ore in a mine, and figuratively any abundant source of something valuable.

clue.text: Søren Kierkegaard, Scooby-Doo, etc?

parts.note: the philosopher is a famous, distinguished man from Denmark
the cartoon dog belongs to a large breed of hound named after Denmark

explanation.walkthrough: Kierkegaard was a celebrated Danish philosopher, so he is one of Denmark's eminent citizens; Scooby-Doo is a dog of the giant breed that shares that description.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase covers both an illustrious person from Denmark and the large mastiff-like dog breed, so the two examples share one label.

clue.text: Socialist employee finally recruited and changed

parts.note: red is the colour of the left, so a socialist is a red

indicators.note: finally points to the very end, so only the closing letter of that word is kept

parts.note: the final letter of this word
a recruit is signed up

explanation.surface: A left-wing worker was eventually taken on and then had a change of heart.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Recruited' looks like the end of a story but it gives the last piece; RED for a socialist is a crossword staple.
explanation.definitionFit: To redesign something is to alter its plan or form, so a redesigned thing has been altered or reworked.

clue.text: Eye's sore? Eyesore, by the sound of it?

indicators.note: the phrase asks the solver to judge by hearing, so a word that sounds alike is wanted

parts.note: a pigsty is a filthy place, and a messy room is called a sty, an eyesore

explanation.surface: A wordplay riddle: is an eye's sore the same as an eyesore?
explanation.walkthrough: The definition and wordplay use the same letters split differently: 'Eye's sore' is the infection, 'Eyesore' is an ugly place, a sty.
explanation.definitionFit: A stye is a small painful inflamed swelling on the eyelid, so it is literally a sore on the eye.

clue.text: Amphibian (English), part of a flower and introduction to taxonomy in set of books

parts.note: a newt is a small amphibian
E is the abbreviation for English
the stamen is the pollen-bearing male organ of a flower

indicators.note: an introduction is the opening, so only the first letter of the following word is kept

parts.note: the opening letter of this word

explanation.surface: A naturalist's reference volumes cover amphibians, flowers and the basics of classification.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a biology textbook, but the set of books is scripture: twenty-seven books of the Christian Bible.
explanation.definitionFit: The second part of the Christian Bible is a collection of twenty-seven books, gospels, letters and Revelation.

clue.text: Our mad racer dashed in heavy vehicle

indicators.note: dashed means smashed to pieces, so the letters are broken up and reassembled

parts.note: taken as written; eleven letters

explanation.surface: A reckless driver of ours has sped off in a big lorry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dashed' reads as hurried, which suits the racer, but it signals that the letters are smashed and rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: A military or security vehicle protected by steel plating is weighty and robust, the kind used by banks and armies.

clue.text: Mounties plan a descent — that includes waterside walks

indicators.note: the phrase says the words before it contain something, so the answer runs inside them

parts.note: runs from the tail of the first word into the start of the last

explanation.surface: Canadian police officers organise a descent down to the shore.
explanation.walkthrough: Mounties are the Royal Canadian Mounted Police; the letters span four words, from mountIES to DEScent.
explanation.definitionFit: An esplanade is a long open level area, typically beside the sea, where people stroll along a promenade.

clue.text: Poet's writing having value

parts.note: writing is made of words
worth is value

explanation.surface: A literary judgement that a certain poet's verse is valuable.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Poet's' looks possessive, but the 's is short for 'is', linking the definition to the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: William Wordsworth was the English Romantic poet who wrote about daffodils and the Lake District.

clue.text: Antarctic explorer: that is, a hairy beast

parts.note: Captain Robert Falcon Scott led the ill-fated race to the South Pole
i.e. is the abbreviation of id est, Latin for that is

explanation.surface: Someone remarks that a polar explorer was a shaggy, unkempt brute.
explanation.walkthrough: The colon makes 'that is' look like an explanation of the explorer, but it supplies the abbreviation i.e.
explanation.definitionFit: A Scottie is a Scottish terrier, a small dog with a wiry, shaggy coat, so a furry animal.

clue.text: So, an African country, a country in Africa

parts.note: taken as written
Mali is a landlocked nation in West Africa
taken as written

explanation.surface: A geography lesson repeats itself, naming one African nation and then another.
explanation.walkthrough: The repetition is deliberate: one nation in the wordplay is embedded inside another in the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Somalia occupies the Horn of Africa on the continent's eastern coast, beside Ethiopia and Kenya.

clue.text: Worker that's absolutely smashing?

parts.note: surface reading: praise for a wonderful employee, smashing being British slang for excellent
setter's reading: a nineteenth-century textile worker who literally broke machines in protest

explanation.walkthrough: Smashing is British slang for terrific; read literally it describes the English workers of 1811 to 1816 who wrecked new textile machinery they feared would cost them jobs.
explanation.definitionFit: The name now also means anyone opposed to new technology, but originally it was one of the frame-breaking weavers.

clue.text: Drunken general: that's swell

indicators.note: someone drunken staggers about in disorder, so the letters reel into a new arrangement

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: An army officer, tipsy, declares that everything is just swell.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Swell' looks like the old slang for splendid, which suits a cheery drunk; it is the verb meaning to grow bigger.
explanation.definitionFit: To enlarge and to swell both mean to grow bigger or expand in size, as a balloon does.

clue.text: Runt led astray, getting to move clumsily

indicators.note: going astray means wandering off the proper course, so the letters stray from their order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: The smallest piglet of the litter wanders off and lumbers about awkwardly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Led astray' reads as one phrase about the runt being misled, but 'led' is fodder and 'astray' alone mixes the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: To trundle is to roll or plod along slowly and heavily, like a cart or a lumbering animal.

clue.text: Round numbers and another number giving you pressure

parts.note: multiples of ten are called round numbers
read as a string of numerals: I (one), O (zero) and N (an unspecified number)

explanation.surface: A maths puzzle where rounding figures and adding one more creates stress.
explanation.walkthrough: The second half is loose: no single number spells the last three letters, so take them as numerals strung together, one, nought and the algebraist's n.
explanation.definitionFit: Tension is mental strain or stress, the feeling of being under pressure, and also physical stretching force.

clue.text: Antipodean with fresh passion ranted madly, losing time

indicators.note: acting madly is acting wildly and without order, so the remaining letters are jumbled
losing something means it goes missing, so a letter drops out of the word

parts.note: fresh means new
zeal is fervent passion
taken as written
T is the abbreviation for time; this letter is removed

explanation.surface: An Australian or Kiwi rants wildly with renewed fervour, running out of time.
explanation.walkthrough: Antipodean means from Australia or New Zealand; take T out of RANTED and mix the five letters left.
explanation.definitionFit: The Antipodes are the lands on the opposite side of the globe from Britain, chiefly Australia and its Pacific neighbour, so a Kiwi qualifies.

clue.text: Seventh of connections Everyman is going to cultivate

indicators.note: seventh names a position, so only the letter standing in that place is kept

parts.note: count along the word to the seventh letter
the setter speaks of himself: Everyman will is I will, shortened to I'll

explanation.surface: The setter announces a plan to nurture contacts, the seventh of his connections.
explanation.walkthrough: Setters often refer to themselves by name, so 'Everyman is going' is the setter saying 'I will', contracted to I'LL.
explanation.definitionFit: To till the land is to prepare and work the soil for crops, which is what farmers do.

clue.text: Workshy person greatly admired, by the sound of it

indicators.note: the phrase asks the solver to judge by hearing, so a word that sounds alike is wanted

parts.note: an idol is someone hero-worshipped

explanation.surface: A lazy celebrity is nonetheless adored, it seems.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Workshy person' looks like one phrase for the definition, but 'person' starts the wordplay; the definition is just the adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: Idle means lazy, avoiding effort, which is what someone reluctant to do any labour is.

clue.text: Stitch? Heck!

definitions.meaning: first meaning: to mend a hole in fabric with needle and thread
second meaning: a mild exclamation of annoyance

explanation.walkthrough: The punctuation makes it look like someone pricking a finger while sewing; the two words are separate senses of one short word.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means repairing a sock with interwoven thread and is also a polite substitute for a stronger curse.

clue.text: Chili brand getting revamp, an original idea

indicators.note: a revamp is a makeover, so the letters are remade in a new arrangement

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A chilli sauce company relaunches its label with a novel concept.
explanation.walkthrough: The marketing story makes 'revamp' look like a business change, but it signals that the ten letters are reworked.
explanation.definitionFit: A brainchild is an invention or plan that someone has thought up personally, their own creative product.

clue.text: Very hot, old London district

parts.note: so means very, as in 'so good'
H is the abbreviation for hot, as on a tap
O is the abbreviation for old

explanation.surface: A description of a sweltering, historic area of the capital.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Very hot, old' reads as a description of the district, but each word gives a separate short piece.
explanation.definitionFit: Soho is an area of London's West End known for its restaurants, theatres and nightlife.

clue.text: British engineer, rather noteworthy, envisaged revolutionary structure launching electronic ecosystem, primarily?

definitions.text: British engineer, rather noteworthy, envisaged revolutionary structure launching electronic ecosystem

indicators.note: primarily means first of all, so the opening letter of each word is the one kept

parts.words: British engineer, rather noteworthy, envisaged revolutionary structure launching electronic ecosystem
parts.note: the initial letters of these ten words

explanation.surface: A tribute to a notable British engineer who imagined a groundbreaking system that started a digital world.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue does double duty: its initials spell the name, and read as a sentence it describes Tim Berners-Lee inventing the World Wide Web.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir Tim Berners-Lee is the British computer scientist who proposed the World Wide Web in 1989 at CERN.
